masthead_title: AT&T beat Wednesday's earnings and raised its outlook — and still fell 6%, the S&P 500's worst performer, on a subscriber miss and new competition from Starlink.
regime_line: This run's week-old bet that the AI-hardware selloff was a durable repricing, not a one-day dip, is now confirmed, even as junk-bond spreads pushed to their loudest flag yet (tightening).

story_html:
The day's two biggest-name stories were both the same pattern: a beat that lost to the guide. AT&T reported Q3 results that beat estimates and raised its 2026 adjusted-EPS outlook to about $2.40 (from $2.25–2.35), a genuinely good quarter by Schaeffer's Investment Research and Invezz's own account — and the stock still fell 6.45% to $21.91, the worst performer in the S&P 500 that session (this system's own close; Schaeffer's and GuruFocus separately put the move near 6%). Multiple outlets (Benzinga, Invezz, FX Leaders) tied the drop to a subscriber miss — 379,000 net new postpaid phone customers against roughly 379,300 expected, down from 432,000 the prior quarter — and to rising competition from SpaceX's Starlink Mobile service; Verizon (−2.48%) and T-Mobile (−3%) fell alongside it on no news of their own (today's concept of the day, below, uses that sympathy move). Netflix told almost the identical story a session earlier: Q3 revenue of $12.87 billion (+12% year over year) and EPS of $0.87 both beat estimates (Deadline, Variety, StockTitan), but the company cut its 2026 advertising-revenue forecast to $2.7 billion from an earlier $3 billion and guided Q4 EPS to $0.67, short of the roughly $0.73 analysts expected — and the stock fell 5.31% to $65.04, a two-year low (this system's own close matches Yahoo Finance's reporting to the cent).

Underneath both stories, this system's own AI-hardware claim resolved. CL-0042, opened a week ago to test whether last Wednesday's AI-hardware selloff was a durable repricing or a one-day rotation, is confirmed (Claims, above): SMH never closed back above the pre-selloff line all week. Super Micro cut against that read on its own, though — its SEC filing dated Oct 20 raised fiscal Q1 2027 revenue guidance to $18.5–19.5 billion from $14.5–15.5 billion, citing stronger AI-server demand, and the stock rose 9.55% (Movers, below). One company's order book and a whole group's stock-price trend are disagreeing, and that disagreement is exactly what Tier 3 exists to track.

The tightening backdrop kept tightening while the headlines were about single stocks. Junk-bond spreads (HY OAS, still dated Tuesday Oct 20 on its one-day lag) widened another 4bp to 3.33%, this run's largest flag for a sixth straight session and now its highest z-score yet (z +3.46) — though the level itself remains below this run's own high of 3.46% set in March, a reminder that an unusually calm recent stretch can make an ordinary level look extreme by the z-score alone. The 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, ticked up 1bp to 5.13%, a level this system hasn't matched outside the current run since July 2007 (today's History check, below, has the rest of that comparison). Credit widening and a broadly higher stock market (S&P +0.58%, Nasdaq +1.05%) pulling in opposite directions, on the same day a chipmaker's own guidance and a stock-price trend disagreed too, is the day's actual regime signal — more than any one earnings call.
dashboard_interp_html:
Treasury yields were mixed and mostly tiny. The 3-month bill fell 1bp to 4.25% (z +1.90; 71st percentile of the last 30 years but only the 52nd since 1962 — unusual lately, ordinary on the fuller record), the 2-year rose 2bp to 4.81% (z +1.78; 83rd percentile of the last 30 years vs. only the 53rd since 1976, a real gap, marked †), the 10-year rose 1bp to 5.13% (z +1.60; 85th percentile of the last 30 years, 48th since 1962, also † — today's lead History-check fact, below), and the 30-year was unchanged at 5.42% and stayed out of flag range (z +1.17; 83rd/47th, † too). The curve was split, not clean: 2s10s narrowed 1bp to 32bp while 3m10y widened 2bp to 88bp, both comfortably un-inverted either way. Why this matters: moves this small don't change mortgage or CD math today; the more useful read is the repeated † gap above — several of these rates are unusual against the last 30 years but unremarkable against six decades, which matters for how much weight to put on “multi-decade high” framing in the press.

Credit is still the loudest flag on the page, and louder than yesterday. HY OAS (the extra yield junk-rated borrowers pay over Treasuries), still dated Tuesday Oct 20 on its one-day publication lag, rose 4bp to 3.33% — this run's largest flag for a sixth straight session, and now its biggest z-score yet (z +3.46; 81st percentile of its own short ~3-year record, §4F — HY OAS doesn't get a 30-year comparison, so there's only the one lens here). The level itself is still below this run's own high, 3.46% last March, so today's news is the z-score, not a new record. IG OAS held flat at 0.87% (z +2.64, the second-largest flag; 56th percentile of its own short ~3-year record, far less stretched than HY). SOFR, the overnight rate banks actually pay each other, rose 1bp to 3.88% (z +2.01; 67th percentile of the last 30 years vs. 45th since 1954, the same lately-vs-historically gap, †). The dollar (DXY) ticked up to 101.78 and stayed out of flag range (z +1.36; 70th percentile of the last 30 years, 80th since 1971). Fed balance-sheet and TGA readings are unchanged from last week's H.4.1/DTS release (thin history, carried forward); ON RRP, the nearly-drained shock absorber between them, rose to $0.24B (z -0.53, not flagged). Why this matters: credit, not the Treasury curve, is this system's best read on whether “tightening” is still orderly, and it widened again today even as stocks rallied broadly — the opposite of what CL-0046's confirm case needs reversed, so the thesis keeps holding one session longer.
history_html:
The 10-year Treasury yield, 5.13%, has sat at or above this level on 16 of 19 sessions since Sep 24; before this run, the last time was July 2007. Only the 48th percentile since 1962, but 85 of every 100 days of the last 30 years — every 1970s/1980s reading sat at or above it too. This run's high, 5.31% on Oct 5, was last matched in May 2002.

2007 shares the yield, not the backdrop. The overnight rate then was 5.26%; SOFR now is 3.88% — a looser Fed landing on nearly the same bond yield. The curve was flatter then (2s10s +19bp, 3m10y +16bp) than today's +32bp/+88bp. Credit (the Baa-10Y proxy, direction only) was a touch wider then (1.59 vs. 1.46). The S&P 500 was at its own record that July day, two months before the 2007-09 crisis; today it's 0.79% below its own record, set three weeks ago.

The real side is more extreme on its narrower record: the 10-year TIPS yield, 2.77% (dated 10-20), sits at or above 99.2 of every 100 days since 2003; before this run, the last comparable reading was November 2008. The Cleveland Fed's model (1982+) cross-checks it: 80th percentile of the last 30 years, only the 54th since 1982 — the same split as above. The 2-year's climb this year (+134bp) is the 9th-largest through this date in 50 years; a rise this size has started eight times since 1977, and the S&P 500 (price only) was lower a year later in 3 of 8 (any 12-month stretch since 1962: 24.4%).

For a client asking whether 2007-level yields mean 2007-level risk: no — the Fed's rate, the curve's shape, and credit spreads all differ, and the one thing that matches (the yield) says less than it feels like it should.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) +9.55% (35.57, from 32.47) — what happened: the second-largest move in today's scan. Stated reason: Super Micro's own SEC 8-K filing, dated 2026-10-20, gave a preliminary update for its fiscal Q1 2027 (quarter ended Sep 30): revenue now estimated at $18.5–19.5 billion, up from prior guidance of $14.5–15.5 billion, and gross margin at 12.0–12.5%, up from 10.4–10.8%, which the filing attributes mainly to higher demand for AI server platforms; the full earnings call is scheduled for Nov 3. Read-through: a direct, company-specific demand signal for the AI-capex build-out (Tier 3, below) — evidence that order books, at least at this one company, haven't slowed even as the broader AI-hardware group (SMH) sits well below its summer high; no position-level view (§8).

AT&T (T) −6.45% (21.91, from 23.42) — what happened: the S&P 500's worst performer today, despite a beat-and-raise quarter. Stated reason: AT&T beat Q3 estimates and raised its 2026 adjusted-EPS outlook to about $2.40 (Schaeffer's Investment Research, Invezz), but added 379,000 postpaid phone subscribers, just short of the roughly 379,300 expected and down from 432,000 last quarter; Benzinga, Invezz and FX Leaders tied the drop to that subscriber number and to rising competition from SpaceX's Starlink Mobile service. Verizon (−2.48%) and T-Mobile (−3%) fell alongside it on no earnings of their own. Read-through: idiosyncratic to telecom competitive dynamics, not a macro signal; today's concept of the day (below) uses the Verizon/T-Mobile sympathy move as its anchor; no position-level view (§8).

Netflix (NFLX) −5.31% (65.04, from 68.69) — what happened: fell to a two-year low the session after reporting, despite beating headline estimates. Stated reason: Netflix beat Q3 estimates (EPS $0.87, revenue $12.87 billion, +12% year over year, in line) but cut its 2026 advertising-revenue forecast to $2.7 billion from an earlier $3 billion and guided Q4 EPS to $0.67, below the roughly $0.73 analysts expected, citing a slower rollout of some ad-product capabilities in its own shareholder letter (Deadline, Variety, Yahoo Finance, StockTitan). Read-through: idiosyncratic — a single company's ad-business and guidance story, not a broad consumer-discretionary signal, though it's the largest single drag behind today's sector note, below; no position-level view (§8).

Sector note — Communication Services (XLC) −1.11% vs. SPY +0.53% (−1.63 points). Netflix, a sizeable XLC holding, fell on its own earnings news (above); AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile all fell too, on AT&T's subscriber miss and the Starlink competition story. Read-through: this sector note is really two single-company stories (streaming guidance, telecom competition) landing in the same sector the same day, not a standalone macro signal about communications broadly.

concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 6
concept_title: Sympathy selling — when one company's news moves its neighbors
concept_html: Not every stock that fell today had bad news of its own. AT&T's 6.45% drop was its own earnings reaction (Movers, above), but Verizon fell 2.48% and T-Mobile fell 3% alongside it, and neither reported results today. That's sympathy selling: one company's news moves its peers even though nothing specific changed about them. The test for whether that's justified, rather than just noise, is whether the news is actually about the group, not only about the one reporter. Here it plausibly is: multiple outlets tied AT&T's subscriber miss to competition from SpaceX's Starlink Mobile service, and that competitive threat applies to Verizon's and T-Mobile's own wireless businesses just as much as AT&T's — a shared, real risk, not sentiment latching onto an unrelated name. Contrast that with Tuesday's Health Care rally (CL-0048, Claims above), where several large health-care names rose together and this system could not find any shared news tying them together at all — that one earned a claims-ledger test precisely because nothing visible connected the names, and it's already reversing after one session. The checklist either way: when a group moves on one member's news, ask what the news is actually about before assuming the whole group deserved the move.
client_translation: When one phone company's earnings report sends the other phone stocks down too, that's not noise -- it usually means investors think whatever hit the one company (here, a new low-cost competitor) is a real threat to all of them, not just a one-company problem.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see AT&T beat earnings and the stock still got crushed?” AT&T's quarter itself was good — it beat estimates and raised its outlook — but it added slightly fewer new phone customers than expected, and analysts pointed to SpaceX's Starlink Mobile as a new, credible competitor. That's different from a bad quarter; it's the market pricing in a new competitive threat for the whole phone industry (Verizon and T-Mobile fell too). Today's concept of the day, above, walks through exactly this kind of move.

“What happened with Netflix? Didn't they just beat earnings too?” Same pattern as AT&T, different cause: Netflix's actual quarter (revenue, profit) beat estimates, but the company cut its advertising-revenue forecast for the rest of the year and guided next quarter's profit below what analysts expected. The stock fell to a two-year low on the guide, not the quarter just reported.

“Should I still be worried about AI stocks after last week's selloff?” Mixed evidence, honestly stated: Super Micro's own filing this week says AI-server demand is still strong enough to raise its revenue guidance by roughly a third. But this system's own test (CL-0042) confirmed today that last week's selloff in that group held for the full week, and junk-bond spreads — one of this system's better reads on financing stress — widened again today even as stocks broadly rallied. Demand looks fine; what it costs to finance the buildout is still the open question.
